extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning set theory / discrete mathematics (readers learning proofs about countability and cardinality)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, definitions, and theorems for proving sets are countable or uncountable, constructing injections/bijections, and comparing cardinalities (including Cantor's diagonal argument and the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem). Targeted at students learning rigorous proofs about cardinality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of countably many countable sets is countable (Theorem 7.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a family of sets, F is countable, and also every element of F is countable, then ∪F is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the family as F = {A1,A2,A3,...} and each Ai as a list Ai = {ai1, ai2, ...}. Note ∪F = {aij | i ∈ Z+, j ∈ Z+}. Define f: Z+ × Z+ → ∪F by f(i,j) = aij; since Z+ × Z+ is denumerable, compose with a bijection g: Z+ → Z+ × Z+ to get an onto map from Z+ to ∪F. Handle the case ∅ ∈ F by removing it (F\{∅}) since the union is unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of finite sequence (Definition 7.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : In → A, where n is a natural number, is called a finite sequence of elements of A, and n is called the length of the sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret finite sequences as functions from an initial segment of positive integers to A; use this to count sequences by counting functions In → A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set of all finite sequences of elements of A is countable (Theorem 7.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is a countable set. Then the set of all finite sequences of elements of A is also countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each n let Sn be sequences of length n. Prove by induction that each Sn is countable: base S0 = {∅}; induction uses the bijection F: Sn × A → Sn+1 given by F(f,a)= f ∪ {(n+1,a)}. Then the set of all finite sequences is ∪n∈N Sn, which is countable by Theorem 7.2.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem: P(Z+) is uncountable (Theorem 7.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no onto function f : Z+ → P(Z+); therefore P(Z+) is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given arbitrary f : Z+ → P(Z+), define D = {n ∈ Z+ | n ∉ f(n)}. Show D ⊆ Z+ but D ∉ Ran(f) by diagonal argument: for any n, n ∈ f(n) ⇒ n ∉ D and vice versa, so D ≠ f(n). Thus no f can be onto; by earlier characterization this implies uncountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonalization technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing an object that differs from each object in a listed family on the diagonal entries to guarantee it is not in the family (used to show non-surjectivity or existence of a new object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the descriptive data (e.g., membership answers) in a table with rows indexed by the listing; read the diagonal entries and flip them to produce a new row that differs from every listed row in at least one position. The textbook calls this diagonalization and notes its broad applicability to many theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: R is uncountable via injection from P(Z+) (Theorem 7.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an injection f : P(Z+) → R to show R is at least as large as P(Z+); since P(Z+) is uncountable, R is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define f(A) ∈ (0,1) by decimal expansion whose nth digit dn = 3 if n ∉ A and dn = 7 if n ∈ A, so f(A)=0.d1d2d3... (using digits 3 and 7 avoids ambiguous repeating-decimal issues). Show f is one-to-one because differing membership at some n gives differing nth decimal digit; argue if R were countable, composition with an injection to Z+ would contradict P(Z+) uncountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of careful digit choices to encode sets as reals
rubrics_metrics.description: When encoding subsets as decimal expansions, pick digits that avoid the standard repeated-decimal ambiguity (e.g., use 3 and 7 rather than 0/9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof of Theorem 7.2.6 uses digits 3 and 7 so each subset maps to a unique decimal expansion; this is a practical anti-pattern avoidance when representing combinatorial data by decimal expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'dominates' notation A ⪯ B and 'strictly dominates' A ≺ B (Definition 7.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: B dominates A (write A ⪯ B) if there is a one-to-one function f : A → B. If A ⪯ B and A ≇ B then A strictly dominates B (writing A ≺ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a preorder (reflexive and transitive) but not antisymmetric. Use this notation to compare sizes when bijections may be hard to construct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem (Theorem 7.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⪯ B and B ⪯ A, then A ∼ B (there exists a one-to-one and onto function h : A → B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem provides a method to conclude equinumerosity from mutual injections even when neither injection is a bijection; the chapter presents a constructive proof to build the bijection h by splitting A into two parts and combining f and g^{-1} appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive method for CSB bijection (proof technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given one-to-one f : A → B and g : B → A, define A1 = A \ Ran(g), An+1 = g(f(An)), X = ⋃n An, Y = A \ X, then define h(a) = f(a) for a∈X and h(a) = g^{-1}(a) for a∈Y. This h is one-to-one and onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scratch work explains why elements outside Ran(g) must go into X, and why the recursive construction ensures consistency. The proof checks injectivity by case analysis and surjectivity by considering g(b) ∈ X or ∈ Y. This is the standard constructive proof used in exercises and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: existence of a rational between reals (Lemma 7.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x < y are real numbers, then there exists a rational number q such that x < q < y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by choosing integer k > 1/(y-x) and using fractional parts m + j/k; use well-ordering principle on suitable set to find j. This lemma is used to prove injectivity of maps from R to P(Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: R ∼ P(Z+) (Theorem 7.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of real numbers is equinumerous with the power set of the positive integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove injections both ways: P(Z+) ⪯ R (earlier theorem) and R ⪯ P(Z+) by composing R → P(Q) via f(x) = {q ∈ Q | q < x} (Lemma ensures injectivity) and then using Q ∼ Z+ and P(Q) ∼ P(Z+) to conclude by transitivity and CSB theorem that R ∼ P(Z+).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set strictly increases cardinality (Cantor's observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, A ≺ P(A); in particular, there are strictly larger cardinalities given by iterating the power set (e.g., Z+ ≺ R ≺ P(R)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantor's theorem shows there is no onto function from A to P(A); exercises and later discussion note that repeated power sets produce infinitely many distinct sizes of infinity. Use this to reason about existence of larger cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical technique: reduce or ignore empty members in family unions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving properties about unions of a family F of sets, if ∅ ∈ F you may remove it (F \ {∅}) because the union is unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 7.2.2 explicitly handles the case ∅ ∈ F by noting ∪F = ∪(F\{∅}) and applying the earlier argument assuming no empty sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using mutually easier injections + CSB to avoid explicit bijection construction (heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a direct bijection is hard to find (e.g., between (0,1] and (0,1)), construct injections both ways and invoke the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook gives (0,1) ⊆ (0,1] trivially and provides f(x)=x/2 as an injection (0,1] → (0,1). Combining these and CSB yields a bijection without constructing it explicitly. This is recommended when explicit matching is tricky.
